category.label: Vitamin D
category.comparisonNote: Vitamin D amounts use IU with micrograms shown alongside (1 µg = 40 IU). Strength comparisons do not specify intake frequency.

guide.title: Vitamin D: deficiency treatment versus routine supplementation
guide.summary: Strength is a unit of amount, not a promise of improved health. The reason for taking vitamin D matters.
guide.evidence: Vitamin D supports calcium regulation and bone health. In generally healthy adults not selected for deficiency, the VITAL fracture study did not demonstrate fewer fractures from supplementation.
guide.limitations: This finding should not be generalized to treatment of diagnosed deficiency or specific bone disorders. A high-strength product is not automatically a better choice.
guide.catalogReading: The catalog shows IU and micrograms together: 1 microgram equals 40 IU. Read the serving size and intended product directions; the comparison unit is not a recommended daily amount.
guide.safety: Excess vitamin D can cause harm, including high blood calcium. Consider existing prescriptions and other supplements before combining products.
guide.author: Supplement Research editorial synthesis
bodySteps: The intestine absorbs vitamin D from food or supplements; skin can also produce it after UVB exposure.
The liver converts it to 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the main blood marker of status.
The kidneys produce its active hormone form, which helps regulate calcium absorption and bone mineral balance.
guide.treatment: Correcting vitamin D deficiency can treat deficiency-related rickets or osteomalacia. It is not a general cure for fatigue, cancer or infections.
guide.whoMayBenefit: People with established deficiency or malabsorption may need treatment. Some groups have routine preventive guidance, including breastfed infants; a pediatric clinician should guide this, not adult catalog strengths.
guide.routineUse: Some people need ongoing supplementation, but the indication and plan differ. A higher-risk group is not proof of an individual deficiency.

whoCanConsider: Adults with diagnosed deficiency following an individualized treatment plan.
People with malabsorption or another recognized risk factor who need assessment of vitamin D intake and status.
whoShouldReview: Kidney disease, hyperparathyroidism or high blood calcium requires medical review.
Thiazide use, strong products or overlapping calcium/vitamin D supplements needs a total-intake check.
buyingGuide.foodSummary: Few foods naturally provide much vitamin D. Fortified foods can contribute; fortification varies by product and country.

value.targetedUse: Clinician-guided correction of an established vitamin D deficiency.
value.reason: Treating deficiency has a strong rationale. Extra supplementation has not shown the same benefit in generally healthy, adequately supplied adults.
worthWhen: There is an established need and an appropriate treatment plan.
Strength, frequency and overlapping sources have been reviewed.
skipWhen: A strong product is chosen solely for general wellness.
Adequate status is assumed to improve further with escalating intake.
value.scope: Targeted rating concerns deficiency treatment. Population-specific preventive guidance and high-strength retail products need separate assessment.

dos.title: Confirm the reason for use
dos.detail: An established need and appropriate care plan matter more than choosing the strongest pack.

dos.title: Check strength and frequency
dos.detail: Read IU, micrograms and product directions, then review vitamin D already present in other products.

donts.title: Don't mistake a comparison for a dose
donts.detail: The catalog's common comparison amount is a price calculation, not your daily intake instruction.

donts.title: Don't escalate for general wellness
donts.detail: Adequate status does not imply that progressively higher intake gives more benefit; excess can cause harm.

intakeGuide.summary: Meet the age- and sex-specific total dietary reference. A reference intake is not the same as a supplemental dose or deficiency-treatment regimen.

limits.label: Vitamin D UL
limits.notes: 4,000 IU/day total intake. A ceiling, not a target; medical replacement regimens require supervision.

notes: No automatic dose increase is assigned for training frequency or experience.

medicalGuide.summary: Condition-specific evidence, separate from sports benefits and purchase priority.

conditions.findings: Correcting deficiency is indicated; treatment and monitoring depend on the diagnosis. Routine high-dose use is not justified by this indication.
conditions.limits: Correcting vitamin D deficiency can treat deficiency-related rickets or osteomalacia. It is not a general cure for fatigue, cancer or infections.

pathway.title: Vitamin D activation: intestine, liver and kidney
pathway.summary: Food and supplements supply vitamin D; skin can also make it after UVB exposure. The main endocrine activation route then involves liver and kidney.

tracks.label: The main activation and signalling route

steps.label: Dietary vitamin D is absorbed
steps.detail: Vitamin D from food or supplements is absorbed in the intestine; the skin provides an additional source.

steps.label: Liver produces circulating 25(OH)D
steps.detail: Liver hydroxylation forms 25(OH)D, the principal circulating marker used to assess vitamin D status.

steps.label: Kidney forms the active hormone
steps.detail: A second hydroxylation, primarily in the kidney, produces 1,25(OH)₂D, also called calcitriol.

steps.label: Calcitriol regulates calcium and phosphate
steps.detail: Active vitamin D promotes intestinal calcium absorption and helps maintain mineral balance needed for bone.

pathway.caveat: This simplified endocrine route does not show every tissue's vitamin D metabolism. Higher supplement doses do not necessarily improve outcomes and can cause harm.
